newsitem.title: USA: U.S. groups urge NAFTA change or repeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. groups urge NAFTA change or repeal.

text.p: A coalition of U.S. labour, environmental and public policy groups released a report on Thursday calling for the North American Free Trade Agreement to be repealed or dramatically changed.

The report said that NAFTA had been good for some North Americans, creating new jobs and protecting U.S. and Canadian investments in Mexico, but the benefits had come at a much greater cost to workers and the environment.
"Wages and living standards have seen downward pressure in all three countries, and workers' rights and bargaining power have been weakened," said the report.

"Damage to the North American environment has intensified," the report said. "Food supplies are increasingly at risk of contamination. The cross-border trade in illegal drugs has accelerated. For the average citizen of any of the three signatory countries, NAFTA has been a failure."
The report was released by the Economic Policy Institute, the Institute for Policy Studies, the International Labour Rights Fund, the Sierra Club and Public Citizen's Global Trade Watch.
It was released ahead of an administration assessment of three years of NAFTA, which joins the United States, Canada and Mexico in a trade bloc, to be sent to Congress next week.
U.S. Trade Representative spokesman Jay Zeigler said it would show that the United States has benefited greatly from the trade agreement.
The debate about NAFTA is important because the Clinton administration plans to seek new legislation in September that would allow it to negotiate expansion of NAFTA to include Chile.
"NAFTA should not be extended, but rather repealed or drastically modified," the report released Thursday said.
The groups argued that many high paying U.S. manufacturing jobs have moved to Mexico as a result of the agreement leading to a sharp rise in the U.S. trade deficit.

The administration has argued that a sharp increase in the U.S. trade deficit with its NAFTA partners in the past three years was due to the robust U.S. economy at a time of slow growth in Canada and an economic crisis in Mexico caused by the collapse of the Mexican peso 1994-95.
But Jeff Faux, president of the Economic Policy Institute, a liberal think tank, said that the rhetoric used to promote the trade agreement before it was enacted into law helped push the peso higher.

"It was in fact the hype of NAFTA that drove the peso up to heights that were not sustainable." Faux told a news conference. "Right now as we speak, the same conditions are recurring. The peso is overvalued, the government is spending money because elections are coming up, it is keeping the peso up ...Sooner or later it has to come down again."
